questions.question: What are the four access modifiers in Java and what does each allow?
questions.title: Java Access Modifiers — private, default, protected, public
questions.direct_answer: Java has four access levels: **`private`** (same class only), **default/package-private** (no keyword — same package), **`protected`** (same package + subclasses), and **`public`** (everywhere). They control visibility of classes, methods, and fields.

interviewer_intent.testing: Core OOP and encapsulation knowledge — interviewers want to see you know why, not just what
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing protected (subclasses from any package) vs default (same package only, regardless of inheritance)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the design principle: use the most restrictive modifier that works (start private, open up as needed)

sections.title: Access Modifier Visibility
sections.content:
| Modifier | Same Class | Same Package | Subclass (other pkg) | Anywhere |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| private | Yes | No | No | No |
| default (no keyword) | Yes | Yes | No | No |
| protected | Yes | Yes | Yes | No |
| public | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

sections.title: Access Modifiers in Practice
How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Java has four access levels going from most restrictive to most open: `private` means only the class itself can use it. Default — when you don't write any modifier — means the same package can access it. `protected` means the same package plus any subclasses, even in different packages. `public` means everyone everywhere. The design principle is to start with the most restrictive modifier that still works — typically make fields `private` and only expose what external code actually needs through `public` methods. This is the foundation of encapsulation.

questions.question: Why should class fields be private in Java, and what is the role of getters and setters?
questions.title: Private Fields with Getters and Setters in Java
questions.direct_answer: Making fields **`private`** enforces **encapsulation** — it prevents external code from directly modifying an object's state in unexpected ways. **Getters** provide controlled read access; **setters** can validate data before accepting a change. This protects data integrity and allows internal implementation to change without breaking external code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of encapsulation as a design principle, not just syntax
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing getters and setters for every field by default — if a field should truly be immutable, no setter should exist
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention validation in setters (e.g., rejecting negative age), and that not every field needs both getter and setter — immutable fields have getters only

sections.title: Encapsulation with Private Fields
Key Points
sections.content:
- `private` fields + `public` getters/setters = the standard **JavaBeans** pattern
- Setters can **validate** input before setting the value
- If a field should never change after construction, provide **only a getter** (no setter)
- Changing internal field names doesn't break external code — only the getter/setter method names matter
- IDEs (IntelliJ, Eclipse) auto-generate getters/setters — but think about whether a setter is actually needed
- `public` fields bypass all protection and are generally bad practice for mutable state

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The reason to make fields private is encapsulation — you're controlling exactly how your object's data can be read and changed. If age is public, anyone can set it to -500 and your object ends up in an invalid state. With a private field and a setter, you can validate the input before accepting it. Getters provide read access. This approach also means if you change how a field is stored internally — say you rename it — external code only depends on the getter/setter method names, so nothing breaks. The key design decision is whether every field needs both a getter and a setter. Immutable fields should have getters only.

questions.question: What is the difference between protected and default (package-private) access in Java?
questions.title: protected vs default Access in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Default** (no modifier) allows access only within the **same package**, regardless of inheritance. **`protected`** allows access within the same package AND from **subclasses in any package**. The key difference: protected crosses package boundaries through inheritance; default does not.

interviewer_intent.testing: The subtlety between protected and default is a common interview trap
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking protected is more restrictive than default, or that default allows subclasses in other packages
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clarify with a concrete cross-package example: a subclass in another package CAN access protected members of the parent, but CANNOT access default members

sections.title: protected vs default — Cross-Package Scenario
protected vs default
sections.content:
| Scenario | default | protected |
|---|---|---|
| Same class | Yes | Yes |
| Same package | Yes | Yes |
| Subclass in SAME package | Yes | Yes |
| Subclass in DIFFERENT package | **No** | **Yes** |
| Non-subclass in different package | No | No |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The difference between protected and default comes down to cross-package inheritance. Default access means only code in the same package can use that member — doesn't matter if it's a subclass or not. Protected adds one more scenario: subclasses in other packages can also access it. So if you have a parent class in package A and a child class in package B, the child can access protected members of the parent, but not default members. Protected is used when you're designing for inheritance — you want to expose certain hooks to subclasses without making them fully public.

questions.question: Can you use access modifiers on local variables inside a method in Java?
questions.title: Access Modifiers on Local Variables in Java
questions.direct_answer: **No** — access modifiers (`private`, `protected`, `public`) cannot be applied to local variables inside a method. Local variables are scoped to the method block and are only accessible within that block anyway. Access modifiers are only for class members (fields, methods, nested classes, constructors) and top-level classes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Precise knowledge of where access modifiers apply — catches candidates who guess
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to make a local variable private or attempting to use static on a local variable
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain WHY — local variables are intrinsically private to the method block; adding an access modifier would be redundant and meaningless

sections.title: Where Access Modifiers Apply
sections.content:
```java
public class Example {
    private int field;      // OK — access modifier on field
    public void method() { // OK — access modifier on method
        // private int local = 5;  // COMPILE ERROR — not allowed
        int local = 5;              // correct — no modifier needed
    }
}
```

Access modifiers control visibility to **other classes** and packages. A local variable is visible only within the block it's declared in — that scope is defined by the curly braces, not by an access modifier.

**Where access modifiers CAN be used**:
- Class fields (instance and static variables)
- Methods
- Constructors
- Nested classes and interfaces
- Top-level classes (`public` or default only)

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Local variables have **block scope** — not accessible outside their `{}` block
- Access modifiers control **external visibility** — irrelevant for locals
- Applying an access modifier to a local variable is a compile error
- `static` also cannot be applied to local variables (another common mistake)
- `final` CAN be applied to local variables — it makes the local a one-time-assign variable

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: No, you can't use access modifiers on local variables. Access modifiers like private and public are about controlling visibility between different parts of your program — they tell other classes whether they can access a member. A local variable inside a method is already completely inaccessible to any other code by definition — its scope is just the enclosing block. So adding an access modifier to a local variable is meaningless, and the compiler just rejects it. The only modifier you can put on a local variable is `final`, which prevents reassignment.

questions.question: What is the most restrictive and least restrictive access modifier in Java?
questions.title: Most and Least Restrictive Access Modifiers in Java
questions.direct_answer: **`private`** is the most restrictive — only the declaring class can access the member. **`public`** is the least restrictive — accessible from anywhere. The order from most to least restrictive is: `private` → default → `protected` → `public`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Quick recall of the access modifier ordering — straightforward but frequently asked
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Placing protected before default in the order — default is more restrictive than protected
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Apply the design principle: always start with the most restrictive access level that makes the code work, then open it up only when needed

sections.title: Access Modifier Order
sections.content:
Access restriction order from **most restrictive** to **least restrictive**:

`private` → `(default)` → `protected` → `public`

```java
private int a;    // most restricted — same class only
int b;            // default — same package
protected int c;  // same package + subclasses in other packages
public int d;     // least restricted — everywhere
```

**Design principle**: Use the most restrictive access that still lets your code work. Only open up access when you have a clear reason. This minimizes coupling between components.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Order: `private < default < protected < public`
- `private` — no other class can access (not even subclasses)
- `default` — package-level sharing; subclasses in other packages can't access
- `protected` — adds inheritance-based access across packages
- `public` — no restrictions
- Principle of least privilege: start private, widen only when necessary
- `private` methods can't be overridden (they're invisible to subclasses)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The most restrictive is `private` — only the class itself can see it. The least restrictive is `public` — everyone everywhere. The order from most to least restrictive is private, then default (no keyword), then protected, then public. The design guideline to go along with this is: start with the most restrictive access that works, and only open it up when there's a specific reason. Making things public prematurely creates tight coupling where other classes start depending on your internals, which makes refactoring painful later.

questions.question: What access modifier comparison matters most: private vs public design decision?
questions.title: private vs public — Design Decision in Java
questions.direct_answer: **`private`** fields with **`public`** methods is the standard OOP encapsulation pattern. Private fields hide state and prevent invalid modifications; public methods form the class's **API contract**. The design rule: hide implementation details, expose behavior through a well-defined interface.

interviewer_intent.testing: Design judgment and OOP maturity — do you understand WHY not just what
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Making everything public for convenience and then having every class depend on your internals
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the API contract concept: public methods are promises to callers; private fields are implementation that can freely change

sections.title: private vs public Design Pattern
private vs public
sections.content:
| Aspect | private | public |
|---|---|---|
| Who can access | Same class only | Everyone |
| Purpose | Hide implementation | Define contract/API |
| Impact of change | No external impact | Breaks callers if changed |
| Use for | Fields, internal helpers | Constructors, main behaviors |
| OOP principle | Encapsulation | Interface design |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The design decision between private and public is really about what's implementation vs what's contract. Your public methods are promises to whoever calls your class — they form the API. Once something is public, changing it breaks callers. Your private fields and helper methods are implementation details — you can change them freely without affecting anyone. The classic pattern is: fields are private (so no one can corrupt your state directly), and you expose behavior through public methods (which can include validation). This separation means you can improve or completely rewrite your internals without breaking any code that uses your class.
